standard.title: Specification for Mobile Containers for Solid Waste — Part 2: Methods of Test (ठोस अपशिष्ट के लिए गतिशील डिब्बे — भाग 2: परीक्षण पद्धतियाँ)
standard.sector: Mechanical Engineering / Material Handling Systems and Equipment

sectional_committee.name: Material Handling Systems and Equipment Sectional Committee

standard.description: This Indian Standard prescribes the methods of tests applicable to mobile containers (waste bins) used for solid waste collection, as described in IS 12402 (Part 1) : 1988, to verify their mechanical strength, structural clearances, impact resistances, thermal durability, and safety under peak load conditions.
standard.scope: This Indian Standard prescribes the methods of tests applicable to mobile containers (waste bins) used for solid waste collection, as described in IS 12402 (Part 1) : 1988, to verify their mechanical strength, structural clearances, impact resistances, thermal durability, and safety under peak load conditions.

certification.description: Mandatory Testing Compliance. Under Municipal Corporation bylaws, state public works department (PWD) guidelines, and solid waste management rules across Indian cities, suppliers of waste management gear must provide test certificates from a NABL-accredited laboratory verifying that their mobile containers successfully withstand the 18-test sequence of IS 12402 (Part 2) before bidding on public tenders.
requirements: Any numerical value representing the final observed or calculated result of a physical dimension, water temperature, deflection percentage, or drop height must be mathematically rounded off in accordance with IS 2:1960. The number of significant places retained should match that of the specified value in the standard.

Before executing any physical tests, a detailed visual inspection of the container must be performed to check that it is completely undamaged, has no manufacturing defects, and to establish a comparison log to measure structural changes.
It must be verified that all structural sizing, nominal volumes, gripping/lifting interfaces, and wheel configurations conform to the specifications of IS 12402 (Part 1).

Containers made of plastic material (entirely or in part) must be conditioned in a temperature chamber prior to physical testing: (a) at -18 ± 3°C for a minimum of 12 hours, and (b) at +60 ± 5°C for a minimum of 12 hours.
Waste containers manufactured entirely of metal are explicitly exempted from undergoing extreme hot or cold thermal chamber conditioning.
For testing normal 'N' type containers, the test ballast density must equal 0.4 kg/dm³ (representing average refuse density of 0.2 kg/dm³ multiplied by a safety factor of 2).
For testing reinforced 'R' type containers, the test ballast density must equal 1.0 kg/dm³ (representing average refuse density of 0.5 kg/dm³ multiplied by a safety factor of 2).
The test ballast must consist of a uniform mix of metal parts (such as long bolts) and rubber balls. The ballast must occupy exactly 90 percent of the total capacity of the container.

Test loads (including container and ballast weight) are strictly calibrated based on volume and type (e.g., 120-litre Type N = 0.48 kN, Type R = 1.20 kN; 240-litre Type N = 0.96 kN, Type R = 2.40 kN; 1000-litre Type N = 4.00 kN, Type R = 10.00 kN).

The standard specifies a strict, progressive sequence of 18 tests (starting with Test 1 check on deflection, Test 2 brim capacity, Test 7 free fall drop, Test 8 inclined impact, up to Test 18 final deflection check) to evaluate progressive structural fatigue.
Under Test 1 and Test 18, the empty container is measured at the gripping plane, and the maximum permissible deflection must not exceed 10/1000 (1.0% of nominal overall width).
Under Test 2, capacity is verified by placing the container level in a receipt tank and filling simultaneously with water at 15 ± 5°C to measure the exact volume of water held at the brim.
Under Test 7, the loaded container is subjected to a vertical drop test consisting of exactly 50 falls (25 falls with the lid closed, 25 falls with the lid open).
Under Test 7, Class A containers (120, 240, 330 litres) must be dropped from a vertical height of 160 mm to simulate rolling off steps and curbs.
Under Test 7, Class B containers (500, 750, 1000 litres) must be dropped from a vertical height of 140 mm (which corresponds to the average height of a standard pavement edge).
After the 50-drop test, the container must show zero permanent deformation, zero weld cracks, and zero damage making it unfit for use. Castors and pivots must remain completely free to rotate.

Under Test 8, the loaded container is mounted on a test truck on a 10° incline and released to strike a rigid wall. It must withstand a total of 80 impacts (across faces 1-4 and edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-1) with a truck travel of 1.0 m (faces) or 0.5 m (edges).
